newsitem.title: UK: POLL-UK rates seen rising for fourth month in row.
newsitem.headline: POLL-UK rates seen rising for fourth month in row.

text.p: British interest rates are likely to rise for the fourth time in as many months as monetary authorities try to prevent a rampant consumer sector from fanning inflationary pressure, a Reuters poll of economists showed on Thursday.

Sixteen of the 23 London-based economists surveyed on July 30 said the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) would put the problem of an overvalued pound on the back burner and raise base rates by 25 basis points to 7.0 percent when it meets on August 6 and 7.

"Despite the risks on the currency side and the risk of further endangering exports, I think the MPC will feel that the strength of domestic demand requires immediate attention," said SE-Banken's chief economist James Stewart.
"The concerns that the MPC had about domestic demand growth last month are still there this month," agreed Mark Ramsden, economist at Stone and McCarthy Research.

Retail sales ballooned by 5.4 percent in June from the same month last year, with windfall payouts from building society flotations encouraging shoppers to hit the high street. On top of that, consumer credit hit record levels in June, surging by 1.275 billion pounds ($2.1 billion).

The other seven economists in the poll reckoned the committee, formed by the Labour government shortly after it came to power in May, would hold off after three consecutive monthly quarter-point rises.
Base interest rates were increased to 6.75 percent at the last MPC meeting on July 10.
"They might sit on their hands because the currency is still quite firm," said Nigel Richardson, international economist at Yamaichi.
"But it's a very fine call whether they decide to go this time or wait a month."
The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) warned against further rate rises after producing figures showing a fall in exports in the four months to July.

A strong pound makes British products more expensive abroad and while sterling's recent meteoric rise has lost its footing in the past few days, economists say it is still overvalued and are waiting to see if this slip signals the start of its downfall.
"(The MPC decision) depends on where the currency is. If we see further falls from these levels and it looks like a trend is developing, then I think they'll raise once more," Richardson said.
But some economists thought the MPC could grab the chance offered by the softening pound and raise rates for the fourth time in a row.
"With sterling coming off against the mark, it's the proverbial window of opportunity," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at Bank of America.
All agreed that further tightening would be necessary before the end of this year and rates could continue on an upward path through to the middle of next.
Economists were split over when the peak would occur. Nine thought rates would rise until around the second quarter of 1998, while nine expected the tightening to cease at the end of 1997.
